edges.effect_quant: A meta-analysis of 4 randomized trials involving 600 pregnant women found that oral bovine lactoferrin improved 4-week hemoglobin change versus oral ferrous salts (mean difference 0.77 g/dL, 95% CI 0.04-1.55) and caused fewer gastrointestinal side effects.
edges.population: pregnant women with iron deficiency anemia treated with oral bovine lactoferrin or oral ferrous salts
edges.mechanism: Lactoferrin can bind and shuttle iron while also modulating intestinal inflammation and hepcidin-related iron handling. In pregnancy, that may allow gentler iron repletion with fewer gastrointestinal side effects than conventional ferrous salts, which can improve adherence as well as iron indices.
edges.summary: Evidence from randomized pregnancy trials suggests lactoferrin can improve hemoglobin and iron markers at least as well as oral ferrous salts, with better tolerability. That makes the overall direction favorable for maternal iron status, especially where ferrous sulfate intolerance limits adherence.
edges.caveats: The evidence base is still fairly small and several trials came from the same research cluster. Reported benefits are clearer for short-term hematologic improvement than for birth outcomes, and the literature includes some retracted studies that should not be used.

evidence.citation: Abu Hashim H et al 2017 Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol
evidence.notes: Lactoferrin or ferrous salts for iron deficiency anemia in pregnancy: A meta-analysis of randomized trials.
